title: Needs and wants
job: Say what you want and don't want
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: un and una are the word for "a", and which one you write is decided by the noun, not by what you mean: un café · una manzana. The plurals unos and unas mean "some".

The article is doing different work in each language. Quiero café asks for coffee as a substance; Quiero un café asks for one cup. English needs a word in front either way — "some coffee", "a coffee" — and Spanish chooses between the bare noun and un.
An adjective normally FOLLOWS its noun: una manzana roja, un café caliente. English puts it in front, always, and that is the order your hand will reach for.

An adjective agrees with the noun it describes, in gender and in number: rojo · roja · rojos · rojas. An adjective ending in -e or in a consonant has one shape for both genders and only goes plural: un café caliente · una sopa caliente · unos cafés calientes.

Gender belongs to the noun and not to its last letter. la leche ends in -e, el día ends in -a, la mano ends in -o, el problema ends in -a. Learn each noun with its article and the ending stops mattering.

A feminine noun beginning with a stressed a- borrows el in the singular, so two stressed a's do not collide: el agua, never la agua. The noun stays feminine and the adjective proves it — el agua fría — and the plural is las aguas.
Negation is one word in front of the verb, and nothing else moves: Quiero café → No quiero café. English has to fetch a "do not" from somewhere; Spanish has nothing to fetch.

A second negative word does not cancel the first. No quiero nada is "I don't want anything": Spanish wants the no in front of the verb AND the nada after it, which is exactly the pairing English forbids.
Wanting to do something is quiero plus the plain infinitive: Quiero comer. There is no word for "to" — Quiero a comer and Quiero que comer are both wrong.
The infinitive is the verb's own name, and its ending sorts it into one of three families: -ar (estudiar) · -er (comer) · -ir (vivir). M4 hangs the person endings on those stems.

words.note: The masculine "a", and the same word as the number one: un café is a coffee and one coffee at once. The feminine is una, and the plurals unos and unas mean "some". The noun's gender picks it.

sentences.trap: M1's Quiero café asks for coffee as a substance. Add un and you have asked for one cup — and English cannot say either sentence without putting a word in front of the noun.
sentences.sound: qu is a plain k and the u is silent: KYEH-ro. un is one short syllable, oon, and it runs straight into the word after it.

variations.changed: drop un and it is coffee in general, not one cup
the ending swaps the person — quiero → quieres
no inside the question — the offer that expects a yes

mistake.why: café is masculine, so its article is un: Quiero un café.

sentences.usage: Ordering, or saying plainly what you want.
sentences.mnemonic: un is "a" and "one" in one word.

sentences.cue: I want a coffee with milk

words.note: "With", and it behaves exactly as the English word does — it sits in front of the thing and changes nothing.
Milk, and feminine: la leche. Its -e tells you nothing about its gender, which is the whole reason a noun is learned with its article.

sentences.trap: The ending is no help at all here: leche is feminine and café is masculine, and neither one ends in -a or -o.
sentences.sound: LE-che, with the ch of "church". Both e's are short and clean, and neither one glides.

variations.changed: no article — milk in general, the way M1 wanted café

variations.cue: Do you want a coffee with milk?
variations.changed: the same words, asked instead of stated

variations.cue: I want a soup with bread
variations.changed: con joins any two — soup with bread this time

mistake.display: Quiero un café con la leche
mistake.why: Milk as an ingredient takes no article: con leche.

sentences.usage: The commonest coffee order in the language.
sentences.mnemonic: café con leche — coffee, with, milk, and nothing in between.

words.note: Bread, masculine: el pan. Like café it is usually taken as a substance, so it stands bare after a verb.

sentences.trap: English builds the negative out of a helper verb — I do not want. Spanish has no helper to build with: put no in front of the verb and stop.
sentences.sound: One short syllable, pahn. The a is the a of "father", cut short, and the n closes it cleanly.

variations.changed: swap the thing refused — the frame is No quiero + the thing
drop the no and it is a want again
swap the verb — no sits in front of whichever verb carries the person

mistake.why: no belongs in front of the verb, not in front of the noun: No quiero pan.

sentences.usage: Turning something down without explaining why.
sentences.mnemonic: One no, straight in front of the verb.

words.note: The feminine "a": una manzana, una casa, una sopa. un and una are one word wearing the noun's gender; the plurals are unos and unas.
Apple, feminine: la manzana (one) · las manzanas (more than one).
Red. It agrees with the noun and comes after it: un libro rojo · una manzana roja · unas manzanas rojas. The -a belongs to the apple, not to whoever is speaking.

sentences.trap: English says "a red apple" and can say it no other way. Spanish says una manzana roja — the adjective goes behind the noun and then copies its gender.
sentences.sound: man-ZA-na. The z is an s across Latin America and a th in most of Spain, exactly as the c of gracias is.

variations.changed: masculine noun, so un and rojo
no article, and both words go plural together

variations.cue: I don't want the red apple
variations.changed: point at that one — la — and refuse it; roja still agrees

mistake.why: The adjective goes after the noun: una manzana roja.

sentences.usage: Choosing between things — at a market, or off a menu.
sentences.mnemonic: Noun first, colour behind it, ending copied.

words.note: necesitar — to need. The -o ending is the "I", as it is in quiero: necesito (I) · necesitas (you) · necesita (he or she). It is the stronger word of the two: a need rather than a wish.
Cold, and it agrees with the noun it describes. Water is feminine, so fría — el agua fría. The article el is only dodging two stressed a's; the -a on the adjective tells you the noun's real gender.

sentences.trap: el agua looks masculine and is not. The article steps aside for the two stressed a's of la agua; the adjective goes on telling the truth — el agua fría.
sentences.sound: FRÍ-a is two syllables, FREE-ah: the written accent splits the i from the a. The r is one light tap.

variations.changed: that particular water — the article is el, the adjective still fría
necesito takes a noun exactly as quiero does
no in front of necesito — refusing a need works exactly like refusing a want

mistake.why: agua is feminine, so the adjective is fría — el agua fría.

sentences.usage: Asking for what you actually need, in a shop or at a table.
sentences.mnemonic: el agua fría — the article borrows, the adjective does not.

words.note: Soup, feminine: la sopa. A bowl of it is una sopa.
Hot. An adjective ending in -e has ONE shape for both genders — un café caliente · una sopa caliente — and only changes for number: calientes. Only the -o/-a adjectives split by gender.

sentences.trap: A large share of Spanish adjectives never show gender at all. caliente is one of them, so una sopa calienta is a word that does not exist.
sentences.sound: ca-LIEN-te, three syllables. The ie is one glide, not two beats.

variations.changed: masculine noun, and caliente does not budge

variations.cue: I don't want the soup cold
variations.changed: refuse it instead — and fría, unlike caliente, does change

variations.cue: Do you want a hot soup?
variations.changed: the offer — same words, and the marks with the tune do the asking

mistake.why: caliente has no feminine form to make: una sopa caliente.

sentences.usage: Ordering food, or sending it back.
sentences.mnemonic: -e adjectives sit still; -o adjectives change clothes.

words.note: To eat — the infinitive, the verb's dictionary name, and the -er says which family. Nothing stands between quiero and it: quiero comer. M4 puts the person endings on the stem: como, comes.

sentences.trap: English "want to eat" has a word for "to" and Spanish has none: the -r on the end of comer is already doing that job.
sentences.sound: co-MER, stressed on the last syllable, and the final r is one quick tap.

variations.changed: any infinitive fits — the frame is quiero + the plain verb
the no goes in front of the verb that carries the ending, not in front of the infinitive
necesito takes the infinitive too — need to eat, want to eat, one frame

mistake.why: No a. The infinitive follows quiero directly: Quiero comer.

sentences.usage: Saying what you want to do, not just what you want.
sentences.mnemonic: The -r on the end IS the "to".

words.note: To study — an -ar verb, the largest family. You already have the noun: un estudiante is a person who does this. M4 turns it into estudio, estudias, estudia.

sentences.trap: Quiero que estudiar copies English's "want that". Spanish wants nothing between the two verbs: Quiero estudiar.
sentences.sound: es-tu-DIAR. The opening e- is the one Spanish always puts in front of s + consonant, exactly as in estudiante.

variations.changed: swap what you study
the no lands on quiero, the verb with the person in it

variations.cue: Do you want to study Spanish?
variations.changed: asked of you — the ending flips to -es and the marks do the rest

mistake.why: There is no que here. Quiero estudiar is the whole sentence.

words.note: querer for tú: quiero (I) · quieres (you) · quiere (he, she and usted). Offering something is this question and nothing else — there is no "do" to put in front of it.

sentences.trap: English needs three words before the noun — do you want. Spanish needs one, and it is the verb itself.
sentences.sound: KYEH-res, stressed on the first syllable, and the final s stays crisp.

variations.changed: an infinitive instead of a noun
usted takes quiere, the he-or-she form
the polite refusal — two words close the offer

mistake.why: Drop the tú — quieres already says "you want". It comes back only to draw a contrast: ¿Y tú, quieres un café?

sentences.usage: Offering something — the most useful question in the module.
sentences.mnemonic: One word does the whole of "do you want": quieres.

words.note: Nothing — and "anything" once a no is already in the sentence. It does not cancel that no; the two work together: No quiero nada. On its own, as an answer, it is "nothing".

sentences.trap: English forbids exactly what Spanish requires. "I don't want nothing" is a mistake in English; No quiero nada is the only way to say it in Spanish.
sentences.sound: NA-da. The d between two vowels is soft, close to the th of "this".

variations.changed: gracias closes a refusal politely
on its own it is a complete answer, and then the no is not needed
swap the verb under the double negative — the frame holds for any verb

mistake.why: The no cannot be dropped in front of the verb: No quiero nada.

sentences.usage: Turning everything down at once — a waiter, a seller, an offer.
sentences.mnemonic: Two negatives, one meaning: no … nada.
